about: Authoritative planning record for the series-architecture layer. Edit by hand, then run `python3 tools/rebuild.py`. Research fields (ideas, territory, place, sources, access, status) are NOT stored here: they come from the lead card named by lead_id. Release order is `seasons[].eps` (lead IDs, in episode order from Episode 2); episode numbers are derived from it. Every season, phase, anchor and chronology position is a proposal unless its status says otherwise.

rejected.SL-SQ24-001: Research direction only. No troupe, village or scheduled performance located, and the form's caste-satire content needs a worked-out position with performers before anything could be filmed.
rejected.SL-SQ21-005: Research direction only. A monument with no identified subject and nothing currently happening.
rejected.SL-SQ24-003: Research direction only. Every source found was a commercial astrology service. No independent evidence of how families actually decide.
rejected.SL-SQ05-002: Single commercial property source. The premise that resident families are being displaced by value is plausible and entirely unevidenced.
rejected.SL-SQ08-006: No working blacksmith located. Encyclopaedic background is not a subject.
rejected.SL-SQ02-003: No living carving practice at or near Embekke established. Without it this is a monument, not a documentary.
rejected.SL-SQ03-008: No human subject with anything at stake. Available material is either promotional or oppositional.
rejected.SL-SQ22-009: No family, association or event identified, and the community's own boundaries are contested within the sources.
rejected.SL-SQ22-002: No seed-keeping farmer identified. Health claims in the trade sources are unusable.
rejected.SL-SQ08-001: Strong subject area, no located subject. A completed technological transition with nobody found who made it.
rejected.SL-SQ16-003: Camps documented only in a personal account and tourism copy. The financing arrangement may involve debt bondage and that was neither confirmed nor excluded; it must not be scheduled on this evidence.

seasons.title: What you notice
seasons.question: What decides what we actually see and hear?
seasons.assumption: That perceiving is passive and complete: that what is in front of a person simply arrives.
seasons.contrasts: A drum maker listening for a tone against a coir worker whose product nobody looks at; a puppeteer's hand that the audience never watches against a bird counter who must take a flock one at a time.
seasons.shift: Attention is an act with a cost, and it selects. By the end of the season the audience has watched several people whose whole skill is a way of attending, and one place where the attending is itself doing damage.
seasons.prepares: If seeing is selective, the next question is what the selection turns things into.
seasons.ep1_effect: Episode 1 was watched before any of this. On a second viewing the monastery sequence reads as somebody learning to attend, not somebody arriving somewhere.

seasons.title: What you take a thing to be
seasons.question: When does recognising something become deciding what it is?
seasons.assumption: That a confident recognition is the same as understanding.
seasons.contrasts: A tune that sells bread without anyone looking at the bread, against a disease recognised by its signs for thirty years with no agreed cause; a guide who sees what a visitor cannot, against a law that turned a way of living into an offence.
seasons.shift: Recognition can be fast, firm, useful and still carry no understanding, and the names it produces can outlast the thing they described.
seasons.prepares: If a name can stick to a person, so can a want. The next season turns to what people reach for.
seasons.ep1_effect: The monastery in Episode 1 is a place the audience recognised instantly. This season makes that instant recognition suspect.

seasons.title: Wanting, having and enough
seasons.question: What keeps something wanted after the cost of it is clear?
seasons.assumption: That wanting is simple, and that people who keep wanting something have not understood what it costs.
seasons.contrasts: Pilgrims who walk for two months carrying almost nothing, against a safari driver whose income depends on producing a leopard; a tea taster whose palate is a calibration, against a freelancer whose income separates them from their street.
seasons.shift: Wanting is not one thing. It can be a reason to go without, a trap built by an incentive, or a measurement against whatever you happen to be used to.
seasons.prepares: Wanting something does not produce the effort to get it. The next season is about what does.
seasons.ep1_effect: Whatever Chathura went to the monastery for, this season makes it harder to call it renunciation.

seasons.title: Effort, readiness and the conditions for acting
seasons.question: What has to be true before a person can act at all?
seasons.assumption: That effort is a matter of will, and that people who do not act have not decided to.
seasons.contrasts: A tapper climbing before the heat against a salt worker who cannot hurry the sun; an ambulance crew whose skill is measured in seconds against a household that has been told its house is unsafe and has not moved.
seasons.shift: Readiness is made of conditions: a body, a season, a price, a road, a rule. Deciding is not moving.
seasons.prepares: If acting depends on conditions, so does learning. The next season asks how anyone can tell they are getting better.
seasons.ep1_effect: Arriving at a monastery is an act with conditions behind it, and Episode 100 will show what they were.

seasons.title: Learning, mastery and the judgement of progress
seasons.question: How do we know whether we are getting anywhere?
seasons.assumption: That progress can be measured, and that someone qualified can tell you where you are.
seasons.contrasts: A dancer whose teacher decides when he may wear the costume, against a lighthouse keeper with nobody to judge him; a ten-year-old sitting a national examination, against a weaving village counting how many households are left.
seasons.shift: Some learning cannot be described, some cannot be examined, and some of what looks like arrival is a place you passed through.
seasons.prepares: Having a skill raises the question of what it is for, and who it is given to.
seasons.ep1_effect: Nothing in Episode 1 tells the audience whether Chathura is a beginner. This season makes that a real question rather than an assumption.

seasons.title: Giving and what moves it
seasons.question: What is actually happening when somebody gives something away?
seasons.assumption: That generosity is self-explanatory, and that the act tells you the reason.
seasons.contrasts: A dansal that gives away everything it makes, against a stall on a mountain trail that is both devotion and a business; a blood donor who gives what they need, against men paid to guard the eggs they used to sell.
seasons.shift: The same act carries different reasons, and some restraint is indistinguishable from generosity until you ask who is watching.
seasons.prepares: Restraint when nobody is watching leads directly to fairness when everybody is.
seasons.ep1_effect: A monastery runs on other people's giving. Episode 1 never shows who fed anyone.

seasons.title: Conscience, fairness and what is shared
seasons.question: How does something held in common become something that can be taken?
seasons.assumption: That unfairness is caused by bad people, and that naming the cause is straightforward.
seasons.contrasts: A river mined at night in breach of a court order, against a village that hands one person the power to open a sluice; a policy decided quickly and paid for over years, against a market where a night's price is taken over from whatever everyone else is doing.
seasons.shift: Division is a process, not a villain. Fear, custom, incentive and a single confident decision all do the work that gets blamed on greed.
seasons.prepares: If fairness is this hard between strangers, the next season asks what it looks like between people who are responsible for each other.
seasons.ep1_effect: Chathura arrives somewhere that is outside all of this, which is a position that has to be paid for by someone.

seasons.title: Care and the limits of helping
seasons.question: When is stepping back a way of caring, and when is it not?
seasons.assumption: That care means closeness, and that more of it is always better.
seasons.contrasts: Keepers who deliberately minimise contact with the animals they are raising, against a woman who leaves the country so that her family can stay in it; a dog that a street half-owns, against a person who has to travel a hundred kilometres to renew a prescription.
seasons.shift: Care has a shape and a limit. Some of it works by withdrawing, some of it never arrives, and some of it is being done by people nobody is looking at.
seasons.prepares: Every one of these relationships ends. The next season is about what that does.
seasons.ep1_effect: Episode 1 shows a person who has stepped away from everyone. This season makes that neither noble nor cold by default.

seasons.title: Loss, ending and what can still be done
seasons.question: What is left to do for something that has already ended?
seasons.assumption: That grief is a phase that closes, and that an answer or a payment can close it.
seasons.contrasts: A family holding an almsgiving for someone who cannot receive it, against families who refuse a sum of money because they were asking a different question; mangroves replanted where a farm destroyed them, against a village now under a reservoir.
seasons.shift: Repair changes the weight of the past without erasing it, and some of what people do after a loss is not repair at all but a way of continuing to attend.
seasons.prepares: If what is gone does not simply close, the last season can ask what continuity actually is.
seasons.ep1_effect: Episode 1 ends with a disappearance. This season teaches the audience not to read a disappearance as an ending.

seasons.title: Change, memory and returning
seasons.question: What makes something still the same thing after everything in it has been replaced?
seasons.assumption: That a place, a craft or a person is a fixed thing that either survives or does not.
seasons.contrasts: A casting method in which the original must be destroyed to make the object, against a workshop in its fifth generation; a coastline that is wearing away, against a railway that stays the same by being continuously replaced.
seasons.shift: Continuity is made of replacement. What returns to a place does not find the place, and the series ends at the end of a line that was destroyed and rebuilt on its own formation.
seasons.prepares: Nothing. This is where the public journey stops and Episode 100 begins.
seasons.ep1_effect: Everything. By this point the audience has been taught that a return is not a recovery, which is exactly the reading Episode 100 needs them to bring to Episode 1.

phases.name: Before the journey is a journey
phases.description: West coast and Colombo: the places reachable without committing to anything.

phases.name: Upward
phases.description: The hill country, Sabaragamuwa and the central districts.

phases.name: Not assigned
phases.description: Island-wide, multi-district or place-not-established stories. No phase is claimed for these.

calendar_conflicts.title: Phase P3 is placed before P4, but its Esala dates fall after the Pada Yatra
calendar_conflicts.detail: The Esala Perahera lead reports the 2025 procession as running from 30 July to 9 August (phase P3). The Pada Yatra lead records a walk of roughly May to July, arriving at Kataragama for the festival (phase P4). In a single year the P3 story happens after the P4 story, which contradicts the proposed phase order. Either the journey spans more than one year, or one of these stories moves phase.
calendar_conflicts.needs: Decide whether the hidden journey spans more than one year, then place both stories.

calendar_conflicts.title: Phase P2 holds dates at opposite ends of the year
calendar_conflicts.detail: Phase P2 contains temple puppet performances recorded as traditionally held in May and June, the Peraliya commemoration on 26 December, and bird ringing recorded in December and February. One pass along the south coast cannot include both May-June and late December without covering at least seven months.
calendar_conflicts.needs: Decide whether P2 is one stay or several visits; do not assign dates until filming is planned.

calendar_conflicts.title: Two northern festivals overlap in August
calendar_conflicts.detail: The Madhu lead records the largest gathering on 15 August in Mannar. The Nallur lead records twenty-five consecutive days in August or September in Jaffna. Both are in phase P5 and may overlap in the same year.
calendar_conflicts.needs: Check the year's festival dates before placing either; they may need separate years or crews.

calendar_conflicts.title: Dated stories with no phase
calendar_conflicts.detail: These stories carry a date or recurring calendar point (for example 28 November, Vesak in May, the March big match) but sit in P7, which claims no position. Their place relative to the other phases and to the framing segments is unknown.
calendar_conflicts.needs: Assign a phase once the places and filming years are known, or leave them unplaced.

calendar_conflicts.title: One journey or several
calendar_conflicts.detail: Taken together the calendar constraints cannot be met in one pass through the island in one year. The owner has not decided whether the hidden journey is one journey over more than one year, or several journeys. Episode 100 depends on this decision.
calendar_conflicts.needs: Owner decision before Episode 100 is planned.

SL-SQ02-001.requirement: A drum has to be followed from the block of wood to a performance in another episode. That means filming the making, marking the specific instrument, and returning to it later.
SL-SQ02-001.audience_first: A craft episode about how a two-toned drum is made.
SL-SQ02-001.ep100_later: The same drum is heard in the Episode 100 reconstruction, which places the making much earlier in the underlying journey than its release position suggests.
SL-SQ02-001.evidence: Drum making at these settlements is reported in published sources seen only as search results. Following one specific drum from the making to a later performance is a production plan and has not happened.

SL-SQ05-001.requirement: A section of the walk has to be travelled with the pilgrims, and the route has to be recognisable again where it crosses other episodes' ground.
SL-SQ05-001.audience_first: A self-contained documentary about a two-month walk.
SL-SQ05-001.ep100_later: The route is the spine of the underlying chronology; Episode 100 shows where Chathura joined it and where he left.
SL-SQ05-001.evidence: The annual pilgrimage is reported in published sources seen only as search results. Joining a section of it, and using its route as the spine of the hidden chronology, are production proposals.

SL-SQ11-001.requirement: The trail has to be climbed in season and revisited out of season, which are two different shoots months apart.
SL-SQ11-001.audience_first: An episode about the people who keep a mountain trail supplied through the night.
SL-SQ11-001.ep100_later: The out-of-season climb is part of the Episode 100 reconstruction, and it is the first time the audience sees the route empty.
SL-SQ11-001.evidence: The season's opening and closing full moons are reported in published sources seen only as search results. The out-of-season climb is a proposed second shoot.

SL-SQ10-001.requirement: A woven piece has to be identifiable, and its later appearance has to be honestly accounted for.
SL-SQ10-001.audience_first: An episode about the last households weaving hana fibre.
SL-SQ10-001.ep100_later: The piece is among the objects gathered in the room in Episode 100 Part A.
SL-SQ10-001.evidence: The weaving is reported in published sources seen only as search results. No piece has been acquired. Its later appearance in Episode 100 would be a production arrangement and must be labelled as one.

SL-SQ16-001.requirement: A specific release has to be filmed, and the same animals looked for afterwards through the monitoring programme.
SL-SQ16-001.audience_first: An episode about raising orphaned elephants for release.
SL-SQ16-001.ep100_later: The return to the park in Episode 100 answers a question the first episode deliberately left open, and may answer it badly.
SL-SQ16-001.evidence: Releases and post-release monitoring by the Department of Wildlife Conservation are reported in published sources seen only as search results. Access to monitoring data, and whether the same animals can be found again, are not established. The return visit is a proposal.

SL-SQ03-005.requirement: No extra filming. The requirement is editorial: several other episodes were filmed in places this cyclone damaged, and that has to be tracked rather than discovered late.
SL-SQ03-005.audience_first: An episode about recovery from a named disaster.
SL-SQ03-005.ep100_later: Episode 100 shows how many of the other episodes sit on one side or the other of this date, which is the only hard chronological marker the series actually has.
SL-SQ03-005.evidence: The cyclone and the damage attributed to it are reported in published sources seen only as search results. Its links to other episodes (CX-010 to CX-012) must be confirmed with the operator or employer. Using its date as the series' chronological marker is a proposal.

SL-SQ20-001.requirement: Upstream and downstream points in the same cascade have to be filmed as one system, in the filling season and again at drawdown.
SL-SQ20-001.audience_first: An episode about restoring an ancient irrigation system.
SL-SQ20-001.ep100_later: The water connects two other episodes that the audience had no reason to connect.
SL-SQ20-001.evidence: Cascade tank systems are reported in published sources seen only as search results. Which cascade any other filming location sits in has not been surveyed, so the physical link between episodes is not established.

SL-SQ18-001.requirement: The commemoration has to be filmed on 26 December, and the same stretch of line filmed on an ordinary day.
SL-SQ18-001.audience_first: An episode about a commemoration twenty-two years after a disaster.
SL-SQ18-001.ep100_later: The ordinary-day footage is used in Episode 100, where the audience finally sees the place without the ceremony.
SL-SQ18-001.evidence: The annual stop on 26 December is reported in published sources seen only as search results. The ordinary-day footage is a proposed second shoot.

SL-SQ22-005.requirement: The line has to be travelled to its terminus, and that footage held back for the release-order ending.
SL-SQ22-005.audience_first: The last episode of the public journey: a train to the end of a rebuilt line.
SL-SQ22-005.ep100_later: Episode 100 reveals that this journey was not the end of anything, and that it happened long before the audience was shown it.
SL-SQ22-005.evidence: The line's destruction and reconstruction are reported in published sources seen only as search results. Holding back the terminus footage for the release-order ending is a production proposal.

idea_differentiation.C003-I02: ST-026 is about the daily climb of a palmyrah tapper in the north, where the sources record the physical risk driving young people away. ST-029 is about a rubber tapper's pre-dawn start in the south-west, where the sources record wages and status driving them away. The body is the site in both, but the pressure on it is different and so is the region and the crop.
idea_differentiation.C009-I01: ST-001 is about attention deliberately steered away from a mechanism: an audience watching a puppet and not the hand. ST-006 is about attention so concentrated on one object that the concentration damages it. One is a craft depending on not being seen; the other is a site being worn by being seen.
idea_differentiation.C011-I02: ST-046 is an inherited institutional routine at a site where the practice is centuries old and the custodial role is formal. ST-047 is a domestic expectation that used to go without saying and is now being renegotiated across distance. One is a rite; the other is an obligation.
idea_differentiation.C020-I01: ST-013 is a condition recognised by its signs for three decades with no agreed cause. ST-017 is a bite that has to be identified in minutes, usually without the animal. Same mechanism, opposite timescales, and in the second case the not-knowing is measurably lethal.
idea_differentiation.C032-I02: ST-062 concerns work that is in plain sight and looked away from. ST-064 concerns distress that is not in sight at all and that the service system is not positioned to find. The first is avoidance; the second is absence.
idea_differentiation.C039-I01: ST-074 is a workshop whose people are replaced generation by generation. ST-077 is a railway whose physical components are replaced continuously. ST-080 is a product whose name survives a change of substance. Person, material and name: three different things being replaced under one appearance.
idea_differentiation.C047-I01: ST-081 is about a sound people remember hearing in a place that may no longer produce it. ST-086 is about villages that are physically under water and can only be remembered. One tests whether a memory still has a referent; the other knows it does not.
idea_differentiation.C052-I01: ST-088 is a raw material held in common that now requires a permit. ST-095 is land in common use that became valuable enough to clear. Material and ground; a licence and a demolition.
idea_differentiation.C055-I01: ST-070 is repair done by hand by the community that lives with the damage. ST-072 is repair ordered by a court against a foreign company. The card's point, that later good changes the weight of the past without erasing it, is tested in the first by labour and in the second by money.
idea_differentiation.C066-I02: ST-068 is about speech that cannot reach a listener because there is no interpreter. ST-071 is about speech addressed to someone who cannot receive it at all. One is a solvable gap; the other is not meant to be solved.
idea_differentiation.C066-I03: ST-076 is a workshop that noticed its age when no new weaver arrived. ST-079 is a coastline whose wearing was masked while it was also accreting. One is a human institution; the other is a physical process, and the second is the card read literally.
idea_differentiation.C073-I03: ST-038 is a skill that lives in the hands and cannot be conveyed in words. ST-039 is a skill gated by permission, where a long apprenticeship precedes being allowed to begin at all. Inarticulable technique and controlled access are different problems.
idea_differentiation.C076-I01: ST-027 is a young woman whose family's sacrifice is domestic and immediate. ST-028 is a doctor whose training was paid for publicly by people they will never meet. Private debt and public investment.
idea_differentiation.C077-I03: ST-023 is a palate calibrated by what it has already tasted, deciding a price. ST-024 is an income measured against the wages of everyone nearby. Sensory calibration and social comparison.
idea_differentiation.C080-I03: ST-089 is a decline attributed to plastic when clay scarcity, cost and labour are also documented. ST-093 is a dispute in which drivers, passengers and platforms each name a different single cause. One is a received explanation; the other is a live argument between parties.
idea_differentiation.C082-I02: ST-055 is an illegal extraction continuing for two decades after a court banned it. ST-057 is a practice inside an institution that renews itself each academic year. Both are escalation, one across time and one across cohorts.
idea_differentiation.C084-I01: ST-014 is a label created by a statute, which converted an existing practice into an offence. ST-015 is a label created by an event, which has outlived the event by more than fifteen years. Law and history, doing the same work to a name.
idea_differentiation.C086-I02: ST-096 is a public argument in which positions are largely taken over from the surrounding discourse. ST-097 is a price that is taken over from what other buyers are doing on the same night. Moral judgement and market judgement.
idea_differentiation.C089-I01: ST-034 is a national shortage of a skill with a harvest window measured in weeks. ST-035 is an individual skill with a window measured in minutes. The scale and the clock are different, and so is who bears the cost of being late.
idea_differentiation.C091-I01: ST-082 is a written script whose readers have gone. ST-087 is a spoken language whose younger speakers can produce the words without using them. Writing and speech, and in the second case the speakers are present.
idea_differentiation.C100-I02: ST-037 is a craft counting how many households still practise it. ST-078 is an institution counting what survived a destruction. One is attrition; the other is a single night.

SL-SQ01-001.title: The hand the audience does not watch
SL-SQ01-001.premise: String-puppet families of the Gamwari lineage in Ambalangoda, Balapitiya and Mirissa make their own puppets and handwritten scripts for Rukada Natya, a UNESCO-inscribed tradition reported to be at risk as younger people move away from it.
SL-SQ01-001.calendar: Performances traditionally at temples in May and June.

SL-SQ01-002.title: What the rope is made of
SL-SQ01-002.premise: In coastal villages of Kalutara where coir craft is documented, the story asks whether fibre is still retted, spun and twisted into rope by hand, and by whom, or whether the work has moved entirely to mills.

SL-SQ01-003.title: The slow way between two towns
SL-SQ01-003.premise: The Hamilton canal, completed in 1802 from the Kelani river to Negombo partly to drain the Muthurajawela wetland, has stretches carrying small boat tours alongside fishing, though the available sources do not describe who uses it or lives on its banks today.

SL-SQ01-004.title: Counting a flock one bird at a time
SL-SQ01-004.premise: Bird ringers and counters work the migratory season in the Bundala and Kumana wetlands, building a record one bird at a time through a national ringing programme launched at Bundala in 2005, with sessions reportedly held in December and February.
SL-SQ01-004.calendar: Migratory season September to March; ringing in December and February.

SL-SQ01-005.title: He points, and you see nothing
SL-SQ01-005.premise: At Sinharaja, a UNESCO World Heritage site, published accounts say every group entering from the two principal entrances must take a guide from a neighbouring village, trained by the Forest Department in what have become sought-after positions.
SL-SQ01-005.calendar: Sinharaja is wettest in the inter-monsoon months.

SL-SQ01-006.title: The looking is what wears it away
SL-SQ01-006.premise: At Sigiriya, conservators and wardens look after frescoes that published accounts describe as the site's most fragile element, with concerns including microbiological growth and vibration from the footfall of the visitors who come to see them.

SL-SQ02-001.title: Two skins, two voices
SL-SQ02-001.premise: Drum makers in settlements near Kandy, including Kuragandeniya in Menikhinna, hollow single blocks of wood and mount two different skins on geta bera and other drums for temples, schools and dancers, amid reported shortages of hides and suitable wood.

SL-SQ02-002.title: Cut with a thumbnail
SL-SQ02-002.premise: Laksha workers apply lac resin to turned wood and, in the niyapoten veda technique, sever it with the thumbnail; published accounts describe a handful of remaining artisans at Hapuwida in Matale, but how many still use it is not established.

SL-SQ02-004.title: Two thousand hectares and one breath
SL-SQ02-004.premise: Monks at Na Uyana Aranya, a forest monastery on the Dummiya range spread over more than 2,000 hectares and described as home to roughly 150 monks, follow a daily routine of alms round, walking and long sitting.
SL-SQ02-004.calendar: Aranyas commonly close to visitors during the rains retreat.

SL-SQ02-005.title: One light and a great deal of sea
SL-SQ02-005.premise: If the offshore Great Basses and Little Basses reef lighthouses, which published accounts state are staffed by keepers, are confirmed still staffed in 2026 and access is granted, the film would follow the keepers' routine and the relief run to the reef.
SL-SQ02-005.calendar: The reef is only approachable in a short calm season.

SL-SQ02-006.title: Watching a very large place with very few people
SL-SQ02-006.premise: Wildlife beat officers and rangers patrolling Yala and Wilpattu work amid reported arrests over a killed pregnant deer, an August 2026 armed confrontation with suspected poachers in Yala, and drought-time poisoning of water holes for meat.

SL-SQ03-001.title: Deciding which way a rough stone faces
SL-SQ03-001.premise: Published accounts report that gem cutters in Ratnapura lapidary shops use the bow-driven hanaporuwa alongside modern Sri Lankan-made machines, and that the traditional method is still prized for cabochon cutting of star sapphires.

SL-SQ03-002.title: A disease known by its signs
SL-SQ03-002.premise: Farming families in the North Central dry zone live with chronic kidney disease of uncertain cause, first reported among paddy farmers in 1994, while researchers studying water, agrochemicals and biomarkers have not reached an agreed cause.

SL-SQ03-003.title: The law that turned a livelihood into an offence
SL-SQ03-003.premise: Reporting records that over sixty years the forested areas the Wanniya-laeto community lived in were converted into sanctuaries, reservoirs and national parks, restricting hunting, honey gathering and chena cultivation for families at Dambana, beside the Maduru Oya National Park.

SL-SQ03-004.title: A word that outlasted the war
SL-SQ03-004.premise: Women heading households in Batticaloa and Ampara are the target of livelihood programmes, while research identifies land ownership rules, lack of formal employment skills and underpayment as constraints, with most such households able to take only low-paid informal or daily work.

SL-SQ03-005.title: A year after the water went down
SL-SQ03-005.premise: Households and institutions hit by Cyclone Ditwah, which made landfall on 28 November 2025 and caused flooding and landslides across all 25 districts, are still recovering, though what that recovery looks like now has not been established.
SL-SQ03-005.calendar: Anniversary of landfall on 28 November; recovery work continuing.

SL-SQ03-006.title: Two hours between the bite and the antivenom
SL-SQ03-006.premise: Peer-reviewed research records that most snakebite patients in Sri Lanka reach a first hospital, usually a small rural one, within an hour, but that a further two hours typically pass before the first dose of antivenom.
SL-SQ03-006.calendar: Bites peak with the paddy calendar.

SL-SQ03-007.title: The tune before the bread
SL-SQ03-007.premise: Across the country, choon paan vendors reportedly leave bakeries before dawn to drive fixed routes in converted three-wheelers and vans, selling bread and short eats to households that come out when they hear the vendor's recurring tune.

SL-SQ04-001.title: Seventeen years to a verdict
SL-SQ04-001.premise: Litigants and remand prisoners wait in a court system that the Ministerial Consultative Committee on Justice recorded in February 2025 as having 1,131,818 pending cases, where criminal prosecutions reportedly take around seventeen years, while a reform package has been proposed.

SL-SQ04-002.title: The thing that waits
SL-SQ04-002.premise: People in residential drug treatment, at centres including those of the National Dangerous Drugs Control Board, are part of a system where reporting records both planned new centres and criticism that some rely on military-style drill rather than treatment.

SL-SQ05-001.title: Two months on foot to Kataragama
SL-SQ05-001.premise: Pilgrims gather in the Jaffna peninsula to walk the Pada Yatra, described as Sri Lanka's oldest annual foot pilgrimage, taking roughly two months down the east coast through Okanda to arrive at Kataragama for the festival.
SL-SQ05-001.calendar: Walk runs roughly May to July, arriving at Kataragama for the festival.

SL-SQ06-001.title: Twenty-five days of a promise
SL-SQ06-001.premise: Over the twenty-five days of the Nallur Kandaswamy temple festival in Jaffna, devotees, including Tamil expatriates returning to fulfil vows, are described as keeping rigorous personal vows, many walking barefoot throughout and some carrying kavadi.
SL-SQ06-001.calendar: Twenty-five days in August or September.

SL-SQ06-002.title: A price decided by a mouthful
SL-SQ06-002.premise: Prices reached each Tuesday and Wednesday at the Colombo tea auction, where tasters and brokers work, feed through the Tea Board's green leaf pricing formula into what smallholder growers are paid a month later.

SL-SQ06-003.title: Earning in a currency your neighbours do not use
SL-SQ06-003.premise: Sri Lankans working online for overseas clients reportedly became liable as service exporters to income tax of up to 15 per cent from 1 April 2025, and reporting records that they lack foreign-currency withdrawal facilities available in neighbouring countries.

SL-SQ06-004.title: The tip that depends on a leopard
SL-SQ06-004.premise: In Yala's Block I, safari jeep drivers and trackers are reported to chase and crowd sightings because many are paid little and depend on tips of USD 50 to 100 when a leopard is seen, as authorities restrict jeep numbers.
SL-SQ06-004.calendar: Yala closes annually for the dry season.

SL-SQ07-001.title: Twenty trees before the heat
SL-SQ07-001.premise: Palmyrah toddy tappers in the Jaffna peninsula climb before dawn in an occupation that reporting describes as facing extinction, with younger people unwilling to take on the risk and co-operatives capping purchases so that sap brings little profit.

SL-SQ07-002.title: The room shared four ways
SL-SQ07-002.premise: Garment workers in the Katunayake free trade zone, described in reporting as young women from the poorer provinces living in crowded boarding houses, earn a reported average of around 35,000 rupees a month against a living-wage estimate of around 94,000.

SL-SQ07-003.title: Trained here, working somewhere else
SL-SQ07-003.premise: Doctors and nurses are leaving the public health service, with figures attributed to the Health Minister reporting 4,642 health workers departing between 2022 and 2025, while the colleagues who stay keep short-staffed wards running.

SL-SQ07-004.title: Three in the morning, every morning
SL-SQ07-004.premise: Rubber tappers and smallholders work through the pre-dawn round as reporting records yields at major plantation companies in 2025 at around half their 2020 level, and tappers leaving over inadequate wages and a lack of social recognition.

SL-SQ08-002.title: You cannot hurry the sun
SL-SQ08-002.premise: Salt pan workers at salterns from Hambantota to Puttalam and Elephant Pass harvest salt made by the sun from seawater, in an industry described as long-established, though whether harvesting is still manual at the main salterns is unconfirmed.

SL-SQ08-004.title: Forty per cent of the milk
SL-SQ08-004.premise: Dairy smallholders make the morning delivery to collection centres of the state company Milco while reported figures put local production at about 40 per cent of liquid milk demand, the rest imported as powder, against a stated government aim of self-sufficiency.

SL-SQ08-005.title: Told your house is not safe
SL-SQ08-005.premise: The National Building Research Organisation reportedly recommended resettling 12,126 families living in high landslide-risk areas, and about 4,700 are reported resettled, leaving the families still there and the unanswered question of why some offered relocation stay.
SL-SQ08-005.calendar: Risk and warnings peak in the monsoon.

SL-SQ08-007.title: Every roof that helps the house strains the line
SL-SQ08-007.premise: Reporting records the Ceylon Electricity Board restricting new rooftop solar connections in high-demand areas where the low-tension network trips from over-voltage, blocking households best placed to invest, while tariffs approved in June 2025 reportedly cut rates by 20 to 40 per cent.

SL-SQ09-001.title: Not enough hands for the bark
SL-SQ09-001.premise: Sector studies and press reporting describe a shortage of roughly 35,000 cinnamon peelers, linked to low pay and social stigma, leaving about 65 per cent of the crop harvested once a year rather than twice, as a training academy trains replacements.

SL-SQ09-002.title: Fifteen minutes and thirty-two seconds
SL-SQ09-002.premise: Emergency medical technicians of the 1990 Suwa Seriya ambulance service, described as launching in 2016 and expanding island-wide, work from dispatch to hospital handover, with a reported average response time of 15 minutes 32 seconds not independently checked.

SL-SQ09-003.title: The night a dancer is allowed to wear it
SL-SQ09-003.premise: Kandyan dance students and their teachers prepare for the ves mangalya, the ritual published accounts describe as granting a male dancer permission to wear the full costume, though whether one is scheduled within a filming window, or may be filmed, is unknown.
SL-SQ09-003.calendar: An initiation happens on a set date.

SL-SQ10-001.title: The last hana weavers of Henawala
SL-SQ10-001.premise: In Henawala, Pata Dumbara, described as the last village in Sri Lanka where hana fibre weaving is still practised, published accounts state about 10 of roughly 95 to 100 families still weave, with several master weavers in their seventies and eighties.

SL-SQ10-002.title: What the fingers know about beeralu
SL-SQ10-002.premise: Women in southern coastal villages such as Magalle, Weligama and Dikwella work beeralu bobbin lace, a colonial-era craft published accounts describe as slowly disappearing because the work is long and arduous, alongside revival efforts including state promotion and fashion labels.

SL-SQ10-003.title: Before you are allowed to write
SL-SQ10-003.premise: A palm-leaf writing tradition that largely ended with printing persists as conservation at the National Library's Preservation and Conservation Centre and in monastic collections, though whether anyone still inscribes new text on ola as working practice is unconfirmed.

SL-SQ10-004.title: The recipe that cannot tell you when
SL-SQ10-004.premise: If a willing lineage holder can be identified, the film would follow holders of paramparika vedakama family medical lineages, described in published accounts as transmitting knowledge through prescriptions on ola-leaf manuscripts, though the one 22-generation claim found is self-reported and uncorroborated.

SL-SQ10-005.title: An exam taken at ten
SL-SQ10-005.premise: Children around ten and their families work through tuition classes toward the Grade 5 scholarship examination, which recent research reports is associated with anxiety, amid a public argument over abolition or reform whose current legal outcome is not established.

SL-SQ10-006.title: Training where there is nothing to train with
SL-SQ10-006.premise: Young athletes and coaches outside the main cities train where peer-reviewed work records sport resources centralised in urban areas and most divisional secretaries lacking sufficient funding to identify talent, though no athlete, coach or club has been identified.
SL-SQ10-006.calendar: School season and the March big match.

SL-SQ10-007.title: The syllables you stop needing
SL-SQ10-007.premise: Nadaswaram and thavil players in Jaffna, including at the Nallur Kandaswamy temple, keep a tradition described as brought from South India, and the question is whether the hereditary line of players continues, with both sources found profiling the same player.

SL-SQ10-008.title: Five grades in one room
SL-SQ10-008.premise: In very small rural schools, some reportedly with 10 to 20 pupils, teachers move between grades as Budget 2025 funds a school-system review and allegations that schools face closure meet a ministry statement that no decision to close any school has been made.

SL-SQ11-001.title: The stalls that stay open all night
SL-SQ11-001.premise: Keepers of tea stalls and shops on the Sri Pada trail, described as open through the night, work a pilgrimage season from the Unduwap full moon in December to Vesak in May, after which the route is described as unlit and unstaffed.
SL-SQ11-001.calendar: Season from the December to the May full moon.

SL-SQ11-002.title: Watering a tree for twenty-three centuries
SL-SQ11-002.premise: At the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi in Anuradhapura, custodians and ritual officers keep what published accounts describe as continuous care of the tree, from cleaning, watering and props to the Duruthu new-rice offering each January.
SL-SQ11-002.calendar: Duruthu new-rice offering in January; observance before the April new year.

SL-SQ11-003.title: An obligation that used to go without saying
SL-SQ11-003.premise: Published demographic work describes Sri Lanka as one of Asia's fastest-ageing populations, and research records that the custom of caring for elders in their adult children's homes is under strain as those children work abroad or far from home.

SL-SQ12-001.title: Paid to be photographed doing it
SL-SQ12-001.premise: At Koggala, stilt fishermen are reported to charge visitors for photographs, some reportedly hiring the stilts from actual fishermen, in a practice described as largely a cultural performance, while some genuine stilt fishing is still said to happen in season.

SL-SQ12-002.title: Giving the thing you need
SL-SQ12-002.premise: Blood donation in Sri Lanka is described as entirely voluntary and unpaid, with published figures putting around 450,000 units a year collected mostly through mobile camps at workplaces, schools and temples, each run by an organiser who has to persuade people.

SL-SQ12-003.title: A stall that gives away everything it makes
SL-SQ12-003.premise: Dansal, temporary Vesak stalls set up by families, businesses, religious organisations and community groups, give away food and drink through volunteers who commonly donate their time and pay for the ingredients, though who funds a large one and what it costs is unknown.

SL-SQ13-001.title: The animal on the other side of the fence
SL-SQ13-001.premise: In dry-zone farming villages, farmers reportedly sleep in raised watch huts beside their fields to guard crops from wild elephants, in a conflict with 1,195 people and 3,484 elephants reported killed between 2015 and 2024.

SL-SQ13-002.title: One shrine, several communities
SL-SQ13-002.premise: The Shrine of Our Lady of Madhu in Mannar, described as drawing Tamil and Sinhala Catholics and Buddhist and Muslim visitors, holds its largest gathering at the 15 August procession, reportedly hundreds of thousands of pilgrims to be fed and housed.

SL-SQ14-001.title: Paid to guard what they used to sell
SL-SQ14-001.premise: At Rekawa, published accounts record that a project begun in 1996 employed former turtle egg collectors as nest protectors and almost all nests were protected; whether protection outlasted the grants that paid for it, and what protectors earn now, is unanswered.

SL-SQ14-002.title: Fifteen nautical miles
SL-SQ14-002.premise: Off Mirissa, blue whales share waters with a busy shipping lane that published analysis says, if moved about 15 nautical miles south, would reduce collision risk by up to 95 per cent, a move the government has been called on to propose.
SL-SQ14-002.calendar: Whale season off the south coast.

SL-SQ15-001.title: What the river is worth by night
SL-SQ15-001.premise: Along the Deduru Oya, newspaper investigation describes more than two decades of illegal sand mining deepening the river bed, eroding banks and damaging livelihoods, despite a 2004 Supreme Court ban that published analysis records as weakly enforced.

SL-SQ15-002.title: What happens underground when nobody is watching
SL-SQ15-002.premise: Around Ratnapura, gem pit miners work on a traditional share system that published accounts describe as small partnerships of investors' money and miners' labour, with finds divided by agreement more often sealed by handshake than on paper.

SL-SQ15-003.title: What the seniors do because the seniors did it
SL-SQ15-003.premise: After a Supreme Court judgment of 9 July 2025 directed at ending ragging in state universities, the Ministry of Higher Education and the University Grants Commission had six months to report back on enforcement, and whether they did has not been checked.

SL-SQ15-004.title: A wire left in a tea estate
SL-SQ15-004.premise: A peer-reviewed study of 17 years of leopard mortality records reports that wire snares accounted for 62.3 per cent of deaths and the central highlands for 46.9 per cent of records, while who sets the snares, and for what, is not established.

SL-SQ16-001.title: Care that has to stay at a distance
SL-SQ16-001.premise: At the Udawalawe Elephant Transit Home, keepers and veterinarians prepare orphaned calves for release with what published accounts describe as deliberately minimal human interaction, though release success and post-release survival rates have not been found.

SL-SQ16-002.title: Leaving with a list of what would bring you back
SL-SQ16-002.premise: The film follows Sri Lankan women leaving for domestic work in the Middle East, and the families they leave, through departure, the household at home, the money transfer and a return, while regional conflict is recorded as discouraging new departures.

SL-SQ17-001.title: Calling something by a name so it can be sent away
SL-SQ17-001.premise: A possible film of a low-country sanni yakuma, the thovil of eighteen masked dances that published accounts say is still held in some households, depends on finding a yakadura and a household with a scheduled ritual, none of which has been identified.

SL-SQ17-002.title: The people who work the mountain nobody looks at
SL-SQ17-002.premise: Around Colombo's dump sites, where a garbage mound at Meethotamulla collapsed in April 2017 killing 32 people, published analysis describes informal waste pickers facing stigma and the informal recycling sector being sidelined as processing plants are built.

SL-SQ17-003.title: The dog you feed and the ones you do not
SL-SQ17-003.premise: A zoned catch-neuter-vaccinate-release programme for free-roaming dogs in Anuradhapura, run from 2021 to 2025, has been evaluated in peer-reviewed work as a national plan to eliminate dog-mediated human rabies reaches its 2026 end, with a 2025 sterilisation allocation reportedly unspent.

SL-SQ17-004.title: Two hundred kilometres for a prescription
SL-SQ17-004.premise: In rural districts where, research records, patients travel 50 to 100 km to renew a psychotropic prescription, the film follows a clinic day, the journey to it, a community counsellor's round and the helpline, against published figures of around 3,000 suicides a year.

SL-SQ18-001.title: The train that stops there every December
SL-SQ18-001.premise: Each 26 December the Ocean Queen Express service, struck by the 2004 tsunami at Peraliya with reported death tolls of around 1,000, stops at the spot as survivors, bereaved families and railway staff gather for a commemoration.

SL-SQ18-002.title: Sixteen beds and the last few weeks
SL-SQ18-002.premise: At Shantha Sevana in Maharagama, described as Sri Lanka's first palliative care unit, which offers free care to terminally ill cancer patients, the film would follow an ordinary week of ward rounds, pain management and family visits, if filming is permitted.

SL-SQ18-003.title: Forty-eight acres of everybody
SL-SQ18-003.premise: At Kanatte General Cemetery in Borella, described as Colombo's main burial ground and crematorium, the film follows the gravediggers, workers and guides who do the same work every day for people who are there once.

SL-SQ18-004.title: When there is nobody to interpret
SL-SQ18-004.premise: The film follows deaf and hard-of-hearing Sri Lankans through classrooms, hospital appointments and a sign language class, in ordinary encounters where meaning does or does not get through amid what published accounts describe as a severe shortage of interpreters.

SL-SQ18-005.title: A sum of money instead of an answer
SL-SQ18-005.premise: Families of the 2019 Easter Sunday victims, principally at St Sebastian's Church in Katuwapitiya, continue a public demand for a prosecution that reporting says successive governments have failed to deliver, while a court has ordered compensation without a conviction.

SL-SQ19-001.title: Planting back into the ponds
SL-SQ19-001.premise: Around Puttalam lagoon, where published research records over half the mangroves cleared for shrimp farming between 1992 and 1998 and more than 90 per cent of former ponds now abandoned, restoration with local communities plants nursery-raised seedlings in and around the derelict ponds.

SL-SQ19-002.title: An offering for someone who cannot receive it
SL-SQ19-002.premise: If a family can be reached through an existing relationship, the film would follow a matakadanaya, the seventh-day almsgiving after a death described in published accounts of Sri Lankan Buddhist funeral practice, with the alms and the monks' visit; no family has been identified.
SL-SQ19-002.calendar: Cannot be planned; depends on a death and an existing relationship.

SL-SQ19-003.title: A billion dollars and the pellets still coming ashore
SL-SQ19-003.premise: The Supreme Court ordered USD 1 billion in compensation for the X-Press Pearl disaster in July 2025, but whether any has been paid or reached a west-coast fisher is unanswered, while beach cleaning continues and buried pellets still wash ashore.

SL-SQ20-001.title: The tanks that were built for a drought nobody alive remembers
SL-SQ20-001.premise: The film follows farmer organisations and restoration programmes desilting, repairing bunds and replanting forest belts in the dry zone's village tank cascades, recognised by the FAO as agricultural heritage, where published accounts describe many tanks as dysfunctional through poor maintenance.
SL-SQ20-001.calendar: Filling and drawdown of the tanks.

SL-SQ21-001.title: Five generations at the same mask bench
SL-SQ21-001.premise: At Ambalangoda, the centre of Sri Lankan mask carving, a workshop that presents itself as held within one family for five generations carves and paints kaduru-wood masks behind its museum, and whether it will pass to another generation is not known.

SL-SQ21-002.title: The model that has to be destroyed
SL-SQ21-002.premise: Published accounts describe family brass workshops in Kandy-district villages such as Pilimathalawa casting lamps, trays and temple fittings, and the premise rests on finding one that still uses full lost-wax casting, in which the original model is destroyed.

SL-SQ21-003.title: The looms are still there
SL-SQ21-003.premise: Press reporting describes family handloom workshops, including in the Thalagune tradition, closing or working at a fraction of capacity after the 2022 economic crisis as loan repayments became unmanageable and skilled weavers migrated, with idle looms beside working ones while demand remains.

SL-SQ21-004.title: A railway that stays the same by being replaced
SL-SQ21-004.premise: The film follows permanent-way and restoration work on the hill-country Main Line to Badulla, including the Demodara loop, with trains running through the worksite after the December 2025 floods, whose recovery Sri Lanka Railways was tracking on a status page.

SL-SQ21-006.title: The building came back
SL-SQ21-006.premise: The Jaffna Public Library, burned on the night of 31 May 1981 with a reported 97,000 volumes including ola-leaf manuscripts, was restored by 2003 but, accounts record, reopened largely without books, and its shelves now show what restoration cannot recover.

SL-SQ21-007.title: The house that used to have a garden in front of it
SL-SQ21-007.premise: Reporting records households along named coasts, including Negombo-Pitipana, Kalutara and Mount Lavinia, losing houses and land to the sea and families relocating in Trincomalee, while sources disagree whether sea sand dredging, structures, sea-level rise or natural processes are responsible.
SL-SQ21-007.calendar: Erosion is worst in the monsoon.

SL-SQ21-008.title: Named after a tree it is mostly no longer made from
SL-SQ21-008.premise: Toddy tappers still climb coconut palms for licensed coastal taverns around Negombo, Kalpitiya and the outskirts of Galle, while published accounts record industrial arrack increasingly made from molasses, leaving open how much arrack sold as coconut arrack comes from palm sap.

SL-SQ22-001.title: Listening for the singing fish
SL-SQ22-001.premise: Whether the reported singing fish of the Batticaloa lagoon, best known from a 1950s recording near the Kallady bridge, can still be heard is unconfirmed, and the film would listen from night boats on a lagoon whose water quality is documented as deteriorating.

SL-SQ22-003.title: A script with fewer and fewer readers
SL-SQ22-003.premise: Arwi, Tamil written in an adapted Arabic script, is described as preserved in manuscripts in Beruwala, Kattankudy and Puttalam, but whether anyone can still read it as a working skill, which would decide whether there is a film, is unknown.

SL-SQ22-004.title: The market that moved and kept its name
SL-SQ22-004.premise: The Manning Market, described as the country's oldest public market, was moved from Pettah to a much larger complex at Peliyagoda in 2020, during the pandemic, and some of its vendors report business has fallen significantly compared with Pettah.

SL-SQ22-005.title: A line put back where it was
SL-SQ22-005.premise: The Northern railway line, destroyed during the war and rebuilt with an Indian government line of credit, reopened to Kankesanthurai in January 2015 and to Talaimannar Pier in March 2015, and the film follows the people who use and maintain it now.

SL-SQ22-007.title: Thirty-two halls left
SL-SQ22-007.premise: The film follows owners, projectionists and audiences at Sri Lanka's remaining cinemas, recorded at around 32 in 2021 after attendance fell from 74.4 million in 1979, where reporting describes screenings cancelled because fewer than ten people attended.

SL-SQ22-008.title: Villages with a water level over them
SL-SQ22-008.premise: Published accounts record about 8,000 families evicted for the Mahaweli programme's Victoria reservoir and 3,200 for Kotmale, and the film looks for those who remember the submerged villages, now ageing, at the reservoir at low water, the memorial and the resettlement colonies.

SL-SQ22-010.title: Words the grandchildren can say but not use
SL-SQ22-010.premise: The film follows Sri Lanka Malay-speaking families in Kirinda, where speakers are reported as a majority, and in Hambantota and Colombo, as published accounts record few children now speaking the endangered creole at home and no support for it in schools.

SL-SQ23-001.title: Permits, cane and a road that used to be busy
SL-SQ23-001.premise: A newspaper investigation, with figures from 2015, reported the cane-craft village of Weweldeniya and Radawadunna, on the Colombo-Kandy road, shrinking from roughly 1,500 families a decade earlier to about 20 active ones, with raw cane requiring government permits.

SL-SQ23-002.title: Blaming the plastic pot
SL-SQ23-002.premise: The potting households of Molagoda, described as one of the oldest continuously active clay-craft communities, work in an industry whose decline published accounts attribute both to plastic and aluminium goods and to clay becoming scarce and expensive.

SL-SQ23-003.title: The turbines and the fishing ground
SL-SQ23-003.premise: On Mannar Island, artisanal fishing communities face a wind farm built along fishing routes in 2020 and a proposed second phase of 52 turbines, with reporting recording fishermen saying they were not told their livelihoods would change and protests blocking the Mannar Bridge.

SL-SQ23-004.title: Whose forest the field is
SL-SQ23-004.premise: In Monaragala district, academic work records chena cultivators reporting wildlife damage, legal action by the Forest Department and drought among their main problems, with around 74 per cent of respondents willing to continue because they have no alternative livelihood.
SL-SQ23-004.calendar: Clearing and burning before the north-east monsoon.

SL-SQ23-006.title: Seventeen hundred and fifty
SL-SQ23-006.premise: Tea plantation workers were reportedly granted 1,750 rupees a day under a January 2026 agreement, 200 rupees of it an attendance allowance that labour advocates warn can still reduce what a worker actually earns.

SL-SQ23-007.title: Who gets to name the reason the fare changed
SL-SQ23-007.premise: In late December 2025, three-wheeler drivers at Ella, Weligama and Sigiriya reportedly protested again against app-based ride-hailing, arguing it erodes their livelihoods, while reporting also records passengers' earlier complaints about meters, fares and reluctance over short trips.

SL-SQ23-008.title: The person who opens the sluice
SL-SQ23-008.premise: Each cultivation season in dry-zone villages with working small tanks begins with farmer organisations and water masters deciding how tank water is allocated, a decision that has to be made and enforced among people who live together.

SL-SQ23-009.title: The land under the settlement
SL-SQ23-009.premise: Families moved from Colombo's underserved settlements into high-rise housing were, published research records, offered standard two-bedroom units regardless of their previous situation, under a programme aiming to free land for commercial development, and what happened to that land has not been checked.

SL-SQ24-002.title: An argument conducted around an animal
SL-SQ24-002.premise: The elephants of the Kandy Esala Perahera, including the Maligawa tusker, are a possible subject, but only if the welfare, regulation, ownership and veterinary oversight behind their use, none of which has yet been documented, can be established.
SL-SQ24-002.calendar: Ten nights ending on the Esala full moon.

SL-SQ24-004.title: The price that is agreed at three in the morning
SL-SQ24-004.premise: At the Dambulla Dedicated Economic Centre, described as the country's largest wholesale vegetable and fruit market, produce is weighed and priced with stall owners acting on commission, though how each night's opening price is set is described differently by the operator and the press.

SL-SQ24-005.title: A decision taken quickly and paid for slowly
SL-SQ24-005.premise: Paddy farmers are still carrying the effects of the synthetic agrochemical ban of April to November 2021, with a 2023 survey reporting an average yield loss of 53 per cent and later reporting describing costlier fertiliser and debt from the period.

SEG-E100A.name: Episode 100 Part A
SEG-E100A.content: The missing events before Episode 1: the crowded-location sequence, the return to the room, the ten accumulated objects shown together, the packing, the motorcycle departure and the travel toward Hunnasgiriya and Meemure, until the existing Episode 1 footage connects.
SEG-E100A.source: User-supplied canon. Not documented anywhere in this repository.

SEG-E001.name: Episode 1
SEG-E001.content: The monastery experience. Ends with Chathura disappearing into the forest.
SEG-E001.source: User-supplied canon. Not documented anywhere in this repository.

SEG-E100B.name: Episode 100 Part B
SEG-E100B.content: Continues from the forest ending: the teacher, the meditation and conversation, and the reconstruction of the larger journey.
SEG-E100B.source: User-supplied canon. Not documented anywhere in this repository.
